'''Rachel Blodgett Adams''' (October 13, 1894–January 22, 1982) was a pioneering American mathematician and one of the first women to earn a doctorate in [[mathematics]] at [[Radcliffe College]] in 1921.

== Biography ==
Rachel Blodgett was born in [[Woburn, Massachusetts]], the oldest of three children of Mabel Edith Owen and William Edward Blodgett, neither of whom attended college.<ref name=":0">Green, Judy, and Jeanne LaDuke. ''[https://www.ams.org/publications/authors/books/postpub/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf Supplementary Material for Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's]''. [[American Mathematical Society]], 2009.</ref>

After graduating from [[Woburn Memorial High School|Woburn High School]] in 1912, she entered [[Wellesley College]] and majored in mathematics and Latin. In addition to her studies, she joined the school's Shakespeare Society and performed cornet in the symphony orchestra. Academically, she was gifted and was named a Wellesley scholar in 1914 and a Durant scholar in 1915.<ref name=":0" /> 

Blodgett graduated with her [[bachelor's degree]] (B.A.) in 1916, and took courses at Harvard that summer. She then moved to [[Montreal|Montreal, Quebec]], Canada to teach math at [[Miss Edgar's and Miss Cramp's School]] until 1918. She then returned to Massachusetts to further pursue her academic and professional endeavors.<ref name=":0" /> 

=== Research ===
For the next three years, Blodgett pursued advanced analysis at [[Radcliffe College]], where she received an Edward Austin scholarship for at least two years and a Mary E. Horton fellowship for her final year. She worked with [[William Fogg Osgood]] and [[Oliver Dimon Kellogg]]. She earned her master's degree  (M.A.) in 1919, and continued on to acquire her Ph.D. in mathematics in 1921.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Rachel Blodgett - The Mathematics Genealogy Project|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=252490|website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|access-date=2020-05-21}}</ref> The following fall term, Dr. Blodgett took a teaching position at [[Wellesley College|Wellesley]].

Rachel Blodgett married Harvard-trained mathematician [[Clarence Raymond Adams]] (1898–1965) on August 17, 1922, in Eden Park, in Providence, Rhode Island. (He was widely known as "C.R. Adams.") At the time, C. R. Adams was a Sheldon traveling fellow from [[Harvard University|Harvard]], which allowed the newly married couple to travel extensively overseas with stops in [[Rome]] and [[Göttingen]], Germany. Upon their return to the U.S. in 1923, the two mathematicians settled down in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], where C. R. established his career at [[Brown University]] and eventually headed the math department there.<ref name=":0" />



Blodgett, now known as '''Dr. Rachel Adams,''' moved forward with her research for a few years, according to mathematician [[Judy Green (mathematician)|Judy Green]],<ref name=":0" /> <blockquote>"At least through the 1920s Adams continued her interest in integral equations. [[Griffith C. Evans|G. C. Evans]] of [[Rice University|Rice Institute]] used information from her dissertation in an extensive review of a book on linear integral equations for the Monthly in 1927. She presented her results to the [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] in 1926 and published them in the ''[[American Journal of Mathematics|American Journal]]'' in 1929."<ref name=":0" /></blockquote>Adams also spent many years tutoring math students at her alma mater, Radcliffe College, from 1926 to 1941, with her friend and colleague [[Mary Graustein]], Ph.D., with the goal of encouraging young female students.<ref name=":0" />

During [[World War II]], Adams registered with the National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel in [[Washington, D.C.]] to help with the war effort, but confirmation of any contribution she may have made as part of that program has not yet been found.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Central Intelligence Agency|url=http://archive.org/details/CIA-RDP67-00059A000300140091-3|title=NATIONAL ROSTER OF SCIENTIFIC AND SPECIALIZED PERSONNEL|date=1947-01-09|others=Emma Best|language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Carmichael|first=Leonard|date=1941-03-07|title=The National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel: A Progress Report|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.93.2410.217|journal=Science|language=en|volume=93|issue=2410|pages=217–219|doi=10.1126/science.93.2410.217|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17775937|bibcode=1941Sci....93..217C |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Later years ===
During their marriage, Rachel and C. R. Adams traveled extensively by automobile in the United States and Europe. The couple never had children. He died in 1965 at the age of 67.<ref name=":0" />

She was 87 when she died in Providence, January 22, 1982.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Pioneering_Women_in_American_Mathematics/IRbOAwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Rachel+Blodgett+Adams+1982&pg=PA119&printsec=frontcover|title=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's|first=Judy|last= Green|first2= Jeanne|last2=LaDuke|year= 2009|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=9780821843765|pages=119-120|chapter=Adams, Rachel (Blodgett)}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
In her estate plans, Rachel bequeathed to [[Wellesley College]] the Blodgett Fund, and stipulated that the fund's income be used for scholarships.<ref name=":0" />

* Blodgett, Rachel. ''The Determination of the Coefficients in Interpolation Formulae: And A Study of the Approximate Solution of Integral Equations''. Dissertation, Radcliffe College, 1921.
